posts.title: Before the hull moves

cards.alt: Before the hull moves. Two separate numerical comparisons show the fixed-state endpoint above its final-window mean: upward fluid force about436 versus217N and bow-up moment about615 versus407N·m. An endpoint is not a time average.

Where the load acts. Aggregate pressure-only vertical contributions at the fixed B endpoint are +897.36 N, −460.39 N and net +436.97 N. These bars show force cancellation, not longitudinal positions, contact-line geometry or a moving response.

Preserve the starting state. A method-only diagram shows that pressure-corrected face-normal flow information must be retained when converting the fixed calculation into a moving-solver restart. It is not a simulated flow field.

Same safeguard. Checked start. Body angular acceleration across internal iterations is about388 then1253rad/s² in the original attempt; its second trial is rejected above the1000limit. Corrected iterations are about388,189and213rad/s². All are within one physical timestep, not a motion history.

A first step. An honest limit. Large9.95microseconds identifies the duration of the one completed numerical timestep. H0 is unchanged. Longer motion, coupled convergence and physical performance have not been demonstrated.

posts.caption:
Before we ask how the hull moves, we need to understand the state we release.

The saved fixed-hull calculation carried a substantial pitching load. Its endpoint was one moment in an unsteady flow, not the same thing as the average over a longer interval.

Our first numerical release stopped inside its first timestep. A controlled diagnostic found missing face-normal flow information in the transfer to the moving solver. Preserving that information allowed one checked step under the same safeguards.

That step spans approximately 9.95 microseconds. It qualifies a startup correction, not stable trim, a completed motion study or rider performance. H0 remains unchanged.

Understanding the start is part of earning the next result.

posts.title: Evidence before speed

cards.alt: Dark graphite cover with monumental 30 and km/h CFD — Completed. Fixed-body preparation; nominal one-second checkpoint; heave and pitch locked. Flow readiness: not yet. Typographic cover, not a field image.
One question at a time. From a 20 to 30 km/h ramp to one controlled speed. Speed held, motion held. Condition the flow, then ask about response. Explanatory experiment sequence, not measured flow.

The solver finished. The engineering didn’t. Genuine recorded drag in newtons and vertical force in newtons versus solver time from about 0.370 to 1.000 seconds. Cyan oscillating traces and dashed window means. Late windows increasingly repeatable; repeatability is one check, not validation.

Why we did not release the board. Heave and pitch remain locked. Recorded bow-up moment about the center of gravity in newton metres versus solver time, about 0.370 to 1.000 seconds. Cyan oscillating trace and dashed window means. Window means still changing; readiness criterion not met. No smoothing.

Evidence before speed. If it is not ready, stop and investigate. Flow development and possible boundary influence remain questions. Cause unresolved; no free release. Do not force the answer you want.

posts.caption:
The solver finished. The engineering question stayed open.

Wahoo’s H0 hull completed a controlled 30 km/h fixed-body preparation run to its nominal one-second checkpoint, with normal exit and an independently checked saved state. Heave and pitch stayed locked throughout.

Earlier work used a 20-to-30 km/h ramp. Holding speed and motion now gives us a more controlled question: is the flow ready before we allow the hull to respond?

Late drag and vertical-fluid-force averages became more repeatable. The instantaneous loads still fluctuated, and the pitch-moment means were still changing beyond the readiness criterion. Numerical completion did not establish flow readiness or physical validation.

So we did not release the board. We are investigating ongoing flow development and possible outlet or boundary influence; the cause remains unresolved. Existing evidence does not yet justify extra CFD duration or a boundary change.

The principle is simple: do not force the answer you want. If the evidence is not ready, stop and investigate.

This is a numerical development milestone, not a stability, rider-test or validated performance result.

This is one unheated synthetic revolution at 3000 RPM over 20 ms, not a power prediction or physical engine validation. The next design questions must account for combined effects, ring support, cooling, manufacturing and fit.

Wahoo Intelligence generated 41 distinct synthetic cylinder-port configurations, then screened all 41 under the same prescribed pressures. The results show how port families, widths and opening times change flow capacity, helping us choose what to investigate next.

A useful contrast: A23-007 and A23-011 show similar outward exhaust totals—534.665 and 537.180 mg—yet first open at 86° and 90°. Similar totals can hide different timing.

Eight designs are shortlisted for the next comparison: five have qualified historical dynamic records to reuse; three await dynamic simulation, proposed for A26. This is a development shortlist, not a ranking of the best engines.

The screen does not predict power, torque, trapped charge, scavenging or rider performance. Mechanical assessment and physical validation are still ahead.

posts.title: The cylinder responds.
posts.caption:
Same exhaust geometry. Different exhaust flow.

That is the interesting connection in Wahoo’s latest simulator milestone. We compared five generated cylinder-port designs with a model that updates cylinder mass and energy, derives pressure and temperature, and feeds the changing state into the next gas-flow calculation.

For G001-01 and G001-05, the exhaust geometry is identical. Changing the transfer-port geometry changes the cylinder response—and the exhaust stream. More flow does not establish a better design.

This is a numerically qualified synthetic study: one initial-value revolution at 3,000 rpm, with zero combustion heat. It is not a physically tested engine or a performance result.

Follow the build as we connect the next pieces.

posts.title: What happens in the first 100 milliseconds?

cards.alt: Graphite Wahoo cover reads “What happens in the first 100 milliseconds?” Large blue 100 leads to a genuine saved H0 geometry view at 100 milliseconds. It is an early numerical study, with actual pose and no magnified motion.

Pale Wahoo card reads “The water pushes back.” An unsmoothed completed-fluid upward-force chart shows all accepted dynamic states and short pulses, with separate lines for native process segments and no restart bridging. A disconnected open dot marks the pre-update release snapshot. The weight reference is 178.5 newtons. Positive fluid force alone does not establish upward acceleration.

Graphite card reads “50 milliseconds. A change in direction.” Actual vertical position falls to a sampled minimum 3.777 millimetres below release at 50.269 milliseconds, then rises to 6.545 millimetres above release at 100 milliseconds. Text qualifies the turn as restart-adjacent and says the bow keeps rotating.

Pale card reads “Less torque. Still rotating.” Separate charts show completed-fluid bow-up moment at current centre of gravity and absolute pitch. The 615 newton metre pre-update release snapshot is labelled and drawn as a disconnected open dot, separate from accepted dynamic states. The endpoint is 0.189 newton metres; pitch increases from 0.411 to 6.529 degrees. Lines break at process segments and the quantities have separate vertical axes.

Graphite card reads “Engineering the next move.” A second genuinely new view of the actual saved H0 surface accompanies the question “What will slow the bow-up rotation?” Text says H0 remains the baseline and makes no optimized hull claim.

posts.caption:
What can one tenth of a second reveal?

In this numerical study at a prescribed 30 km/h, H0 first moves down, then rises. Its sampled low point is at 50.269 ms, close to a process restart; accepted neighboring samples support the reversal, while that timing retains the restart qualification.

The bow keeps rotating upward. The fluid moment about the current centre of gravity falls from a 615 N·m pre-release snapshot to 0.189 N·m at 100 ms, but a small remaining torque does not erase momentum gained earlier. Absolute pitch reaches 6.529°, with bow-up rotation still continuing at 1.381 rad/s.

Curves show accepted dynamic states. Open dots mark the separate release snapshots; lines break at process restarts.

That is a useful development finding, not stable trim or a finished hull. This is the dry, provisional-inertia H0 model with a closed intake, no rider and no thrust. It has not been physically validated. H0 remains our baseline while the next engineering question is reviewed.

What will slow that rotation?

Torque opposes. Rotation continues.

At 150 milliseconds in H0’s early simulation, an opposing pitching moment is braking the bow-up rotation. Pitch rate is about 16.7% lower than at 100 ms, yet the bow is still rotating upward. Slowing and stopping are different observations.

The hull is also still rising and accelerating upward. Stable trim and qualified damping remain open questions.

This is numerical evidence at imposed 30 km/h, with unchanged H0 geometry: a dry, closed-intake model with no rider or jet thrust and provisional inertia. It is not physical validation or a product-performance result. Actual restart pulses remain in the graphs; nothing has been smoothed away. Completed-fluid moments and applied body loads have different coupling clocks.

The next move is to use that evidence to frame controlled hull-design and intake-integration questions. Proposed changes still need testing.

posts.caption:
Water will get in. What happens next?

Real riding experience keeps bringing us back to that question. Splashing and capsizing make water ingress part of the design problem for a gasoline jetboard.

In our new H1-02 digital study, we removed the direct enclosed duct between the external air nozzle and engine. That duct could collect water and direct it toward the engine. The original green nozzle now feeds an open engine compartment, with engine induction kept separate.

A simpler air arrangement still needs a water-management plan. Where water collects changes as the board tilts, and the engine, exhaust, fuel, electronics and jet pump all compete for space. Our preliminary bilge layout uses a recovered project pump shape; the actual hardware and its capability are not selected.

Next we are developing the inner structure, connected drainage, component packaging and service access. Fuel-tank and battery installation remain unresolved. Airflow, drainage effectiveness and physical installation still need qualification; this is not a finished waterproofing or water-ingestion prevention solution.

posts.title: Moving is not yet settled

cards.alt: Dark CFD milestone card with the exact saved 100 ms H0 underside pressure field. Legend minus 15 to plus 6 kPa, native p relative to zero Pa. At 100 ms absolute bow-up pitch is 6.529 degrees and heave is plus 6.545 mm from release. Accepted numerical history, not a physical test.

Dark CFD card with actual absolute bow-up pitch increasing over zero to 150 ms on a zero to 12 degree scale. All 4,042 source rows retained, with process-restart breaks. Headline: The angle keeps growing. Stable trim and damping remain unproven. H0 retained while H1 concepts develop.

posts.caption:
A hull moves. The forces change. The next question emerges.

Our early H0 dynamic CFD milestones captured the first 100 and 150 milliseconds at an imposed 30 km/h. By 100 ms the hull had risen 6.545 mm from release and reached 6.529 degrees absolute bow-up pitch.

At 150 ms, bow-up rotation was slowing: pitch rate fell from 1.381 to 1.150 rad/s between 100 and 150 ms. But the pitch angle continued increasing, reaching 10.229 degrees. Slower rotation is an observation of this numerical history; stable trim and hydrodynamic damping have not been demonstrated.

H0 remains our preserved numerical baseline while H1 concepts develop the internal architecture. Controlled comparisons remain a future, separately authorized step.

These are accepted numerical observations, not physical prototype test results. Graphs retain all 4,042 saved samples, split at process restarts without smoothing. No engine output, rider behavior or final product performance is established.
